source: Wang et al. (2024) Planning in Natural Language Improves LLM Search for Code Generation (PlanSearch)
finding: Searching over different natural-language plans (a difference-forcing operator on ideas) raised correctness at a fixed number of attempts, most on the hard, contamination-free benchmark. Gap 1: yes for correctness, at equal attempts.
numbers: LiveCodeBench pass@200, repeated sampling vs IdeaSearch vs PlanSearch: GPT-4o-mini 53.3/59.4/64.9; GPT-4o 60.6/70.4/73.0; DeepSeek-Coder-V2 53.2/65.9/70.3; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 55.6/70.2/77.0. HumanEval+ Claude 88.9/95.6/98.5. MBPP+ Claude 83.0/87.8/93.7. o1-mini LCB 90.8/91.2/91.3 (gain nearly gone).
quote: PLANSEARCH explores a significantly more diverse range of potential solutions compared to baseline search methods.
limits: Equal attempts (k), not equal tokens: planning costs extra tokens per attempt. The paper says compute-normalised plots (Appendix D) give highly similar findings; I did not read those plots. Needs a verifier (unit tests) to pick the winner. Code tasks only.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence that forcing different ideas, not just different wording, raises the chance that one attempt is correct. Gain shrinks for a model that already searches (o1-mini).

source: Wang et al. (2024) PlanSearch: idea-diversity score and pass@1 cost
finding: Gap 2: the descriptor that predicts search gain is the idea, judged by an LLM on pairs of programs. Token entropy is called insufficient. PlanSearch often lowers pass@1 while raising pass@k.
numbers: Diversity D = 1 minus the fraction of program pairs an LLM calls 'same idea' (subset of 40 programs for large n). Relative gain pass@1 to pass@200 tracks D across models and methods on the same dataset (Figure 6, a plot; no correlation coefficient in the text I read). PlanSearch hurts pass@1 for several models, e.g. Sonnet 3.5 on LiveCodeBench.
quote: While entropy is a common diversity measure, it is oftentimes insufficient for LLM settings.
limits: Diversity score uses an LLM judge (judge error not reported in the parts I read). Correlation is across a handful of model-method points on one dataset. Post-hoc measure, not used as a search signal.
agent_relevance: Use an approach-level descriptor (what is the idea) rather than embedding distance or answer-string distance. Expect single-attempt accuracy to dip while best-of-k rises, so judge by coverage at k.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Huxley-Godel Machine: selection by clade performance
finding: Gap 3: the score of a node alone is a weak guide to which node to expand. An estimator that pools the results of a node's descendants (clade) predicts later success far better than the greedy scores used by DGM and SICA.
numbers: Pearson correlation with empirical clade metaproductivity, SWE-Verified-60 (weighted): SICA 0.444, DGM 0.285, HGM 0.778; Polyglot weighted: 0.274, 0.383, 0.626; unweighted HGM 0.512 (SWE-Verified-60) and 0.873 (Polyglot; text prints 0.8783).
limits: The target is defined by the authors and built from the same tree; they remove leaked nodes, but the benchmark is theirs. One group, one setup.
agent_relevance: When choosing which earlier attempt to extend, value it by how well its branch did, not by its own score. This is a goal-plus-future-progress blend, not a novelty term.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Huxley-Godel Machine: head-to-head with DGM and SICA under one setup
finding: Gap 8 (partial): a different group (Schmidhuber lab) re-ran the Darwin Godel Machine as a baseline with cheaper backbones. DGM did improve its starting agent, so its core claim holds in direction, but HGM beat it.
numbers: Same start (40% SWE-Verified-60; 20.3% Polyglot), 800 evaluations. SWE-Verified-60: SICA 50.0, DGM 53.3, HGM 56.7. Polyglot: SICA 25.4, DGM 27.1, HGM 30.5. CPU-hours Polyglot: DGM 2385, HGM 347 (6.86x faster). Full SWE-Verified 500 tasks, 8000 evaluations: HGM agent 61.4%.
quote: all three methods successfully perform agent discovery by optimizing the initial agent through self-improvement
limits: Backbones differ from the original DGM (GPT-5 / GPT-5-mini; Qwen3-Coder), 60-task subsets, so the original DGM numbers (20 to 50, 14.2 to 30.7) are not reproduced. Table text was garbled in extraction; row labels checked against the prose (6.86x = 2385/347). A rival method paper, not a neutral replication.
agent_relevance: Archive-based self-improvement does lift an agent in a second lab's hands, but with smaller, setup-dependent gains.

source: Song, Kempe, Munos (2025) Outcome-based Exploration for LLM Reasoning
finding: Gaps 1 and 3: a novelty bonus on final answers (rare answers get a bonus) raises pass@k and keeps diversity in RL training, but only in the version with a baseline. A naive UCB bonus helped training reward and mostly not test performance.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen-2.5-7B-Base, MATH and DAPO data, 3 seeds, 32 samples per question. Naive UCB: significant test gain only for Llama on the easy set. UCB-Con and UCB-Mean (bonus with baseline) improve test pass@k across models and datasets. Table gains are small: Qwen pass@1 about 0.38-0.42 and pass@32 about 0.62-0.64 across methods; best-checkpoint differences about 0.01 pass@1.
quote: strikingly, RL can reduce effective diversity even on the training set relative to the base model
limits: Training-time method, not a prompt-time scaffold. I could not map every table row to its method from the extracted text, so table numbers are approximate. Gains are small relative to seed spread in places. Math only.
agent_relevance: A novelty term on the answer class works when the descriptor is the final answer (few classes) and the goal reward stays. Pure novelty alone is not tested.

source: He, Fried, Welleck (2025) Rewarding the Unlikely: Lifting GRPO Beyond Distribution Sharpening
finding: Gaps 1 and 3: goal-only RL (GRPO) sharpens the model onto already likely proofs and can lose to simply sampling more from the base model at large N. A reward for rare-but-correct solutions raises pass@N.
numbers: Lean theorem proving, DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-SFT start. Correct proofs of 9600 attempts: GRPO-Epochs-2 8008 (+153), Epochs-3 8006 (+301), Unlikeliness-1 8023 (+299), Unlikeliness-2 8065 (+316); one more variant +358 (rows partly misaligned in extraction; check before quoting). Final recipe competitive with DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL on miniF2F-test.
quote: unlikeliness reward, a simple method for explicitly up-weighting rare but correct solutions
limits: Perfect verifier (Lean). Formal proof only. Training-time.
agent_relevance: Novelty helps when tied to correctness: reward unlikely AND correct, not unlikely alone. Matches the blend idea of gap 3.

source: Yue et al. (2025) Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
finding: Gaps 6 and 1: goal-only RL narrows coverage. RL models win at k=1 but base models win at large k, so much of the gain is sampling efficiency, and diversity is what gets lost.
numbers: Across model families and math/code/visual benchmarks. Example: Minerva, 32B, base beats the RL model by about 9 points at k=128. An Oat-Zero/DAPO RL model started nearly 30 points above base, then was surpassed. pass@256 falls as RL training goes on. Six RLVR algorithms perform similarly. Distillation does expand the boundary.
quote: base models consistently catch up to and eventually surpass RL-trained models
limits: About RL training, not prompting. Pass@k with a perfect check, so it reflects coverage, not what a single answer gets.
agent_relevance: Supports a scaffold that keeps several different attempts alive: coverage lives in the diversity of the base distribution, and a pure correctness push can destroy it.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Gaps 4 and 1: coverage (any sample right) keeps growing with the number of samples, roughly log-linear, but picking the right sample without a verifier stalls. More attempts only help if you can recognise the good one.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 (single-sample SOTA 43%). CodeContests Gemma-2B: 0.02% at 1 sample to 7.1% at 10,000. MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, but majority vote or reward model went only from 40.50% to 41.41%.
limits: Independent samples, no difference operator, no archive. Shows the ceiling for any novelty method that cannot verify.
agent_relevance: A novelty operator raises coverage; the scaffold also needs a verifier. Several hundred is where unverified selection stops paying.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Gap 7: keeping and expanding stored partial solutions, with the option to drop dead ends and return to the parent, beat restarting from scratch on a puzzle where early steps decide failure.
numbers: Game of 24, GPT-4: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC k=100 9.0%, CoT best of 100 49%, IO best of 100 33%, IO+refine 27%; ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. About 60% of CoT samples already fail after the first step.
quote: around 60% of CoT samples already failed the task after generating the first step
limits: Search is breadth-first with an LLM value check (sure/maybe/impossible), not a return to a stored state chosen by novelty. Experiments done 5-16 May 2023 on one model; small tasks with a checkable answer.
agent_relevance: Return-to-partial-state search beats extra independent samples on tasks where the first move decides. Not a test of novelty-guided return.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Game of 24 cost table
finding: Gap 7 equal-token check: ToT spends more than the sampling baselines it beats, so the comparison is not at equal tokens.
numbers: Per case, Game of 24: IO best of 100 1.8k prompt / 1.0k completion tokens, $0.13, 33%; CoT best of 100 6.7k / 2.2k, $0.47, 49%; ToT 5.5k / 1.4k, $0.74, 74%. Creative writing: ToT about 5x completion tokens and cost.
limits: Column alignment of the extracted table is my reading; success column agrees with Table 2. GPT-4 prices of May 2023. No token-matched curve in the paper.
agent_relevance: Return-to-partial search gives a gain per dollar here (74% at $0.74 vs 49% at $0.47) but the paper never shows an equal-token curve, so gap 7 is only partly closed.

source: Peeperkorn, Kouwenhoven, Brown, Jordanous (2024) Is Temperature the Creativity Parameter of Large Language Models?
finding: Gap 6: raising temperature gives only slightly more novel text and more incoherence. No link to typicality or cohesion.
numbers: Llama 2-Chat 70B, one fixed prompt. 100 stories at each of 7 temperatures for the computational analysis; human study: 5 stories per temperature plus the greedy exemplar = 31 stories, 5 per participant. Temperature weakly correlated with novelty, moderately with incoherence, not with cohesion or typicality.
quote: temperature is weakly correlated with novelty, and unsurprisingly, moderately correlated with incoherence
limits: One model, one prompt type (short stories), 31 human-rated stories, non-expert raters who disagree often. Paper warns results may not transfer.
agent_relevance: Do not use temperature as the difference operator. It buys little novelty and costs coherence; structured difference (distinct plans, distinct answers) is the better lever.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (Infinity-Chat), intra-model results
finding: Gap 6: even aggressive sampling does not make one model's answers differ in meaning. Noise is not exploration.
numbers: Infinity-Chat: 26,070 open-ended and 8,817 closed-ended real queries; 100-query subset; 70+ models. With min-p sampling (top-p 1.0, min-p 0.1) at temperature 2.0, average pairwise embedding similarity among responses to the same prompt typically exceeds 0.8 (text-embedding-3-small). 31,250 human labels, 25 raters per item.
quote: even under maximally aggressive sampling, LMs still fail to generate diverse responses
limits: Embedding similarity is itself a descriptor with known weaknesses. Open-ended chat queries, not reasoning tasks.
agent_relevance: Supports a forced difference (condition on past attempts, or a different approach label) instead of random sampling.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: inter-model homogeneity and judge calibration
finding: Gaps 5 and 6: different models give nearly the same answers, so a second model is a weak source of difference. LLM judges and reward models agree less with humans exactly where answers are similar in quality or humans disagree.
numbers: Inter-model similarity: DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82, DeepSeek-V3 vs gpt-4o 0.81. Judge study: 50 prompts x 15 responses x 25 ratings = 18,750 absolute labels; 12,500 pairwise labels. 56 LMs, reward models and judges compared with humans by Spearman correlation; correlations notably lower on similar-quality and high-disagreement subsets (coefficients are in a figure, not read as numbers).
limits: Open-ended queries, not tasks with a right answer. Coefficients not extracted.
agent_relevance: A self-judge of whether something is new will be weakest in the cases that matter (similar-looking attempts). Use external checks where possible.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: Gap 5: an LLM judging its own output is biased toward it, and the bias tracks how well it recognises its own text.
numbers: News summaries (two datasets, 1,000 articles each). GPT-4 is 73.5% accurate at picking itself out against two other LLMs and humans; all three models above 50% untuned; GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 above 90% after fine-tuning on 500 examples. Self-preference strength rises linearly with self-recognition.
quote: Self-preference strength is linearly correlated with self-recognition.
limits: Summarisation, 2023 models. Linear fit shown as a figure. Causal evidence comes from fine-tuning experiments.
agent_relevance: A same-model judge of its own novelty will tend to rate its own attempts well. Errors can enter the archive. Prefer a different judge or an external test.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? judge-versus-human section
finding: Gap 5: LLM judges are poorly calibrated at absolute scoring but give some signal when comparing two items. Human experts also agree only a little above chance on the same task.
numbers: 1,200 ICLR 2024 LLM-related submissions, accepted vs rejected pairs: Claude-3.5-Sonnet 71.4%, GPT-4o 61.1%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%. Human reviewer agreement in the idea study 56.1% (NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment 66.0%; chance 50%).
limits: Predicting paper acceptance is not predicting novelty. Pairwise format helps; direct scoring was poorly calibrated.
agent_relevance: If the agent judges novelty, use pairwise comparison against named earlier attempts, and expect roughly 30% error.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Gaps 5 and 9: ideas that judges rated more novel lose much of that advantage once carried out. Judged novelty does not equal useful progress.
numbers: 43 expert researchers each executed one randomly assigned idea (over 100 hours each), blind expert review. Score change from ideation to execution: human ideas novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052; AI ideas -1.049, -1.760, -1.879 (1-10 scale). Larger drops for AI on all four metrics (p<0.05, FDR corrected). Rankings flip on several metrics.
quote: scores of the LLM-generated ideas decrease significantly more than expert-written ideas
limits: 43 projects, NLP prompting ideas, one template.
agent_relevance: Novelty judged before the work is done overstates value. Check difference by outcome, not by how the idea reads.

source: Burda, Edwards, Pathak, Storkey, Darrell, Efros (2018) Large-Scale Study of Curiosity-Driven Learning (noisy TV)
finding: Gap 9: a surprise signal is drawn to a source of pure randomness. In a Unity maze with a TV that changes channel on action, learning slowed a lot, though agents sometimes still reached the extrinsic reward after long runs.
numbers: Figure-only result (IDF and RF, with and without TV); no numeric table in the text. Authors saw the effect only in a purpose-built environment, not in their games.
quote: the presence of the TV drastically slows down learning
limits: Prediction-error curiosity, not archive novelty; qualitative figure; one maze.
agent_relevance: In text, the noisy TV is any source of free difference: rephrasing, new wording, random detail. A difference operator needs a descriptor that ignores those.
